title: if and else

youtube.title: C++ if and else: Make Your Program Decide | C++ Programming EP 13
youtube.description: In this episode you will write an if statement, add an else branch and use braces around every branch, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 if and else · 1:20 Pass or fail · 2:22 Two paths · 3:11 Second program · 4:24 Recap · 4:54 Bug of the Day · 5:55 Challenge · 6:22 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "IF OR ELSE?" in tomato on cream; Xecxec next to a road that splits into two paths; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a road that splits into two paths

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today your program learns to decide. It tests a condition, and then it takes one of two paths.

scenes.onScreen: "if and else": numbered lines (1. An if statement tests a condition; 2. The body runs only when the test is true; 3. Else runs when the test is false) and an analogy card: a fork in the road: the sign decides which way you walk
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: An if statement tests a condition. If the condition is true, the body runs. If it is false, the body is skipped. Add an else branch for the false case. Exactly one branch runs. Think of a fork in the road. A sign says which way to walk, and you never take both paths. Every program you use makes decisions. A phone checks the password before it opens. A bank app checks your balance before it pays. All of this starts with a plain if. The curly braces hold the body of each branch. Even for one line, write the braces. They stop many mistakes when you add a second line later.
points: An if statement tests a condition
The body runs only when the test is true
Else runs when the test is false

analogy.title: if and else
analogy.body: A fork in the road: the sign decides which way you walk

scenes.onScreen: result.cpp: an if and else branch decide on a mark
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] Marks is seventy-two. [HL 6] The if tests whether marks is at least thirty-five. The test sits inside round brackets. [HL 7] The test is true, so this line runs and prints Pass. [HL 8] The else branch is skipped. [HL 9] It would print Fail, but only for a mark below thirty-five. [HL 6] The test must give true or false. Here, the comparison gives a bool, and that is exactly what if needs. [HL 7] This line runs only when the test is true. Our marks are above thirty-five, so the program prints Pass. [HL 8] Notice that else has no test of its own. It means, in all other cases. [HL 9] Change marks to thirty, and this line runs instead.

scenes.onScreen: a decision tree: the test, and the true and false paths
scenes.animation: Nodes pop in one by one; edges draw on as the narrator mentions them
scenes.narration: Here is the decision as a tree. The test is at the top. If it is true, we follow the left path and print Pass. If it is false, we follow the right path and print Fail. The program never follows both paths. Notice that only one path runs in each run of the program. The other path stays silent, and the computer does not even look at it. A tree like this is a good way to plan code before you type it.

diagram.caption: a decision tree: the test, and the true and false paths

scenes.onScreen: parity.cpp: the remainder decides if a number is even or odd
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Cin reads a number. [HL 7] An even number has remainder zero when we divide by two. [HL 8] That branch prints even. [HL 9] Seven has remainder one, so the else branch runs. [HL 10] The program prints seven is odd. [HL 7] The remainder of a number divided by two tells us if the number is even. Every even number gives zero, and every odd number gives one. [HL 10] You can use this trick for any test on odd and even, such as seats in a bus.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as parity dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. Type seven and press Enter. The program prints seven is odd. Try more numbers. Type ten, and then type zero. Zero is even, because the remainder is zero.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. An if statement tests a condition. Two. The body runs only when the test is true. Three. Else runs when the test is false. Four. Always use braces, even for one line. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: An if statement tests a condition.
The body runs only when the test is true.
Else runs when the test is false.
Always use braces, even for one line.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A semicolon after the if
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the g++ warning appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the warning goes away with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. A semicolon sits after the if test. C plus plus reads it as an empty body. The block below then always runs. With marks equal to twenty, the program would still print Pass. The compiler warns about an empty body. Remove the semicolon. This mistake is hard to see, because the code looks almost right. The semicolon ends the if statement early. The braces then belong to nothing, and they run every time. So read every if line slowly, and look at the end of the line.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the if statement break up with else? It said, you are always my second choice.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the if statement break up with else? It said, you are always my second choice.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: decide if a number is positive
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Read a number. Print positive if it is greater than zero, and not positive in all other cases. Hint: the test is the number greater than zero, and the else branch covers zero and all negative numbers. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: else if ladders. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (a warning, the program still builds):

result.cpp: In function 'int main()':
result.cpp:6:21: warning: suggest braces around empty body in an 'if' statement [-Wempty-body]
    6 |     if (marks >= 35);
      |                     ^
bug.why: A semicolon after the test is an empty body. The block below it is then an ordinary block, and it always runs.

challengeAnswer: Use cin to read n. Test n greater than zero. Print positive in the if branch, and not positive in the else branch.
